title: Separable Rank of Radial Kernels: Machine-Checked Characterization in Lean 4 and Applications
abstract: Filtering an image or three-dimensional wave field directly with a round (radially symmetric) kernel K(x) = phi(||x||^2) of width W costs W^d multiply-adds per output sample. When a 2-D kernel is a product h(x_0)v(x_1) of a horizontal and a vertical 1-D filter, it can instead be applied as two cheap 1-D passes; the separable rank R is the smallest number of such coordinate-product terms needed to sum to K. On a d-dimensional grid, rank R reduces W^d taps to d R W one-dimensional taps per sample (for example, a 9-tap-wide 3-D stencil drops from 9^3 = 729 taps to 3 x 4 x 9 = 108 taps when R = 4). Ordinary bell-shaped Gaussians exp(-alpha ||x||^2) have rank 1, but cannot form flat-top camera defocus disks or ringed wave stencils; practical designs therefore sum damped radial waves exp(-alpha ||x||^2) cos(omega ||x||^2 + theta) (complex-rate Gaussians), or more generally polynomials in s = ||x||^2 times real or complex exponentials (exponential polynomials). We determine which continuous radial kernels on R^d (d >= 2) have finite separable rank, and how many product terms each requires. First, K(x) = phi(||x||^2) has finite rank if and only if phi(s) (s >= 0) is a finite sum of exponential polynomials; conversely, decaying complex-rate Gaussians with one shared width and equally spaced frequencies can approximate any continuous radial kernel that fades to zero at large radius. Second, for a pure complex-rate Gaussian (deg P = 0) in d dimensions, expanding real and imaginary parts naively takes sum_{2 | q} C(d, q) = 2^{d-1} real products (4 in 3-D), whereas an alternating angle-sampling identity achieves the exact minimum of d real products (3 in 3-D); for general polynomial degree k = deg P >= 0, exact real rank is (d - 1)k + 1 per real exponential (1 at k = 0, d at k = 1, 2d - 1 at k = 2) and 2(d - 1)k + d per complex-conjugate pair (d at k = 0, 3d - 2 = 7 in 3-D at k = 1). Third, allowing sequences of lower-rank kernels that converge uniformly on compact sets (compact-open border rank) never lowers rank in 2-D, whereas in d >= 3 dimensions it strictly reduces the cost of polynomial-weighted profiles: for ||x||^2 cos(||x||^2) in 3-D, exact real rank is 7, limits of radial Gaussians take 6 terms, and general real separable limits take 5, at the cost of O(h^{-1})--O(h^{-3}) cancelling weights in finite precision. All 32 mathematical theorems are verified by the Lean 4 proof assistant, and reproducible Python/Triton case studies examine finite-grid discretization, 16-bit (float16) conditioning, and GPU crossovers on an RTX 4070 Ti Super: across 20 HDR bokeh scenes (R = 12), orthogonalizing 2-D filter terms cuts max float16 sRGB error from 7.90 +/- 0.92/255 (8.18 +/- 0.92/255 under magnitude reordering alone) to 0.31 +/- 0.13/255, and in 3-D acoustics (256^3 voxels), exact 3-term-per-Gaussian stencils cut step time by 24% over naive 4-term expansion (1.51 +/- 0.03 ms vs. 1.98 +/- 0.02 ms; fourth-order 25-point FDTD takes 0.325 +/- 0.0002 ms/step on the same grid, or an estimated 52x--71x more runtime and 40x more memory when grid-refined to match 0.1% dispersion) while keeping directional wave-speed error below 0.2% in spatially varying media where 1-step cuFFT does not apply. Code, proofs, and data are public domain (CC0 1.0) at https://github.com/OlliNiemitalo/kernel-rank-lean.
